t.2.75.1: Then, through the night that heralds the auspicious day, the bards and minstrels, masters of eloquent speech, praised Bharata with hymns full of auspicious blessings.
t.2.75.2: Struck with a golden drumstick, the watch-drum sounded forth, and by the hundreds they blew conches and sounded instruments of high and low tones.
t.2.75.3: That very great sound of musical instruments, as if filling the heavens, tormented Bharata, already burning with grief, still more with sorrows.
t.2.75.4: Then Bharata, awakened, stilled that clamor, and saying, "I am not the king," he spoke these words to Śatrughna.
t.2.75.5: Look, Śatrughna, at the great harm done to the world by Kaikeyī: King Daśaratha has gone, leaving his sorrows upon me.
t.2.75.6: This royal fortune of that great-souled king of righteousness, rooted in dharma, now drifts aimlessly like a rudderless boat upon the water.
t.2.75.7: Then, seeing Bharata thus lamenting, bereft of his senses, all the women wept piteously and aloud.
t.2.75.8: While he was lamenting thus, the greatly renowned Vasiṣṭha, knower of the duties of kings, entered the assembly hall of the lord of the Ikṣvākus.
t.2.75.10: He who knew all the Vedas seated himself upon a golden seat spread with a most costly covering, and gave instructions to the messengers.
t.2.75.9: The righteous-souled one, together with his retinue, entered the delightful hall made of gold and crowded with gems and jewels, as though it were Sudharmā.
t.2.75.12: Then a great tumultuous uproar arose from the people approaching with chariots, horses and elephants.
t.2.75.11: Without delay and with composure, bring here the brāhmaṇas, the kṣatriyas, the warriors, the ministers and the leaders favoured by the people, for we have urgent business to attend to.
t.2.75.13: Then the subjects welcomed Bharata as he arrived, just as they had welcomed Daśaratha, as the immortals welcome Śatakratu.
t.2.75.14: Like a lake teeming with whales and serpents, its waters still, its bed strewn with gems, conches and gravel, the assembly hall, graced by the son of Daśaratha, shone as it had of old, as though Daśaratha himself were present.
